items.readable_text:
Content:
So far, we have considered the area of a right triangle.
But what is the area of a general triangle, one that is not necessarily a right triangle?

Content:
It turns out that the same idea still works.

Content:
> A formula for the area of a triangle is
> [MATH: \textrm{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot b \cdot h,]
> where [MATH: b] is the base and [MATH: h] is the corresponding height.

Content:
This formula works for any triangle.

Content:
Let's use this formula to find the area of the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/454e981a2c41f61be2352b56e4c13604]

Content:
In our triangle,
[MATH: \textrm{base} = 7 \: \text{ft}, \qquad \textrm{height} = 3 \: \text{ft}.]

Content:
Therefore, the area of the triangle is
[MATH: Area|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 7 ⋅ 3; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 21; = 10.5ft^{2}.]

Content:
At the end of this lesson, we'll show how to prove the formula for the area of a triangle.

Content:
Let’s see more examples.

sections.normalized_html: Find the area of the triangle.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find the height and base of the triangle: [MATH: base|= 6; height|= 4]

The area of the triangle can be found by the following formula: [MATH: \textrm{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \textrm{base} \times \textrm{height}]

Substituting the values of the base and height, we get [MATH: Area|= (1)/(2) × 7 × 4; = (1)/(2) × 28; = 14.]

Now, let's find the units. Since base and height are measured in inches, the area is measured in square inches. Hence, [MATH: \textrm{Area} = 14 \, \textrm{in}^2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's write down what we know:

[MATH: Height = 8; Area = 30]

The area of the triangle can be found by the following formula: [MATH: \textrm{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \textrm{base} \times \textrm{height}]

Substituting the values of the area and height, we get [MATH: 30|= (1)/(2) × base × 8; 30|= 4 × base.]

Using the relationship between multiplication and division, we get [MATH: \textrm{base} = 30 \div 4 = \dfrac{30}{4} = \dfrac{15}{2}.]

Now, let's find the units. Since the area is measured in square meters and the height is measured in meters, the base is measured in meters. Hence, [MATH: \textrm{base} = \dfrac{15}{2}\, \textrm{m}.]
